questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with severe pemphigus vulgaris refractory to corticosteroids and azathioprine is started on rituximab. What is the primary structural composition of rituximab that distinguishes it as a chimeric monoclonal antibody?
opts: Fully murine variable and constant regions derived from mouse hybridomas
Murine variable regions (Fab) with human constant regions (Fc), approximately 75% human and 25% mouse
Fully humanized antibody produced in transgenic mice expressing human immunoglobulin genes
Human variable regions paired with chimeric constant regions from multiple species
questions.exp: Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody composed of murine-derived variable light and heavy chain regions (Fab portion) responsible for CD20 antigen recognition, paired with human IgG1 constant regions (Fc portion). This approximately 75% human, 25% mouse composition is designed to reduce immunogenicity compared to fully murine antibodies while maintaining targeting specificity.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male with severe nodulocystic acne unresponsive to multiple courses of oral antibiotics is started on isotretinoin. Which of the following best explains isotretinoin's unique efficacy in acne compared to other systemic retinoids?
opts: It binds strongly to all RAR and RXR subtypes, activating gene transcription
It induces sebocyte apoptosis and reduces sebaceous gland size by up to 90%, directly suppressing sebum production and Propionibacterium acnes
It acts as a panagonist with potent anti-inflammatory effects on leukocyte subsets
It undergoes reverse esterification in the presence of dietary lipids, prolonging its tissue half-life
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is uniquely sebosuppressive and does not rely on clear binding to known retinoid receptors; instead, it likely acts as a prodrug while exerting its primary therapeutic effect through direct sebocyte apoptosis and dramatic reduction of sebaceous gland size. This mechanism, which reduces sebum production and secondary bacterial colonization, is not shared by acitretin or alitretinoin and enables isotretinoin to induce long-term acne remission.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple rough, dome-shaped papules on his hands and fingers with characteristic black dots on the surface. Histology shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and pathognomonic 'church spire' projections with koilocytes in the upper stratum spinosum. Which HPV type is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: HPV 3
HPV 1
HPV 10
HPV 28
questions.exp: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) are caused by HPV 1, 2, 4, 27, or 57. The clinical description of exophytic dome-shaped papules with thrombosed capillary loops (black dots), plus the histological hallmark of koilocytes and 'church spire' architecture, is pathognomonic for common warts. HPV types 3, 10, and 28/29 cause flat warts, which lack papillomatosis and have a different clinical presentation.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CHURCH made of SPIRES piercing the SKY—each spire is a pointed keratin projection in common warts caused by HPV-1,2,4 (the 'common' crowd).

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with symmetric, shiny erythema and superficial scaling on the balls of his feet and heel. The interdigital web spaces are completely spared. Which of the following best explains the pathognomonic sparing pattern in juvenile plantar dermatosis?
opts: Interdigital spaces have thicker stratum corneum that resists maceration
Weight-bearing surfaces experience cyclic wet-dry transitions while web spaces remain consistently humid in occlusive footwear
Fungal infections preferentially colonize weight-bearing areas
The instep has higher sebaceous gland density protecting against irritant dermatitis
questions.exp: Juvenile plantar dermatosis is driven by repeated cycles of maceration (from sweat in occlusive footwear) followed by rapid drying in weight-bearing areas. The interdigital web spaces and non-weight-bearing instep remain constantly humid inside shoes, preventing the damaging wet-dry transition. This pathophysiology explains why these areas are characteristically spared, making the absolute sparing of toe clefts the primary distinguishing feature from tinea pedis.

questions.q: A mother with a history of recurrent genital herpes presents in active labor at term. What is the approximate risk of neonatal HSV transmission?
opts: Less than 1-3%
questions.exp: Mothers with recurrent genital herpes at delivery carry a much lower transmission risk of less than 1-3%, largely because they have protective transplacental maternal antibodies from previous infections. In contrast, primary infection near delivery carries a catastrophic 30-50% transmission risk due to high viral shedding and absent maternal antibodies.

questions.q: Which of the following historical landmarks correctly matches the person or event to donovanosis?
opts: McLeod first described the condition as a 'serpiginous ulcer' in Chennai, India in 1882, and Major Charles Donovan identified Donovan bodies in 1905
Major Charles Donovan first recognized the disease in 1882 and described it as a 'chronic venereal sore'
Pund and Greenblatt identified the causative organism in 1905 from cultures on artificial media
Greenblatt et al. in 1939 first isolated Klebsiella granulomatis from human blood cultures
questions.exp: McLeod recognized donovanosis in Chennai, India in 1882 and described it as a 'serpiginous ulcer.' Major Charles Donovan, working in Madras (Chennai) in 1905, identified the causative agent—the Donovan bodies—in exudates from an oral lesion. Pund and Greenblatt described pathognomonic 'cells of Greenblatt' in 1937, and Greenblatt et al. achieved experimental reproduction of lesions in 1939.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: McLeod (1882) saw the SERPENT ULCER wiggling through Chennai streets → Donovan (1905) RODE in on a horse and caught the body inside a vacuole—timeline locked!

questions.q: A 28-week pregnant woman is referred for ultrasound assessment after her Hutterite community clinic noted decreased fetal movements and polyhydramnios. The fetus is born at 31 weeks with profound skin rigidity, microstomia, and joint contractures. Which statement about the genetic epidemiology of restrictive dermopathy is correct?
opts: The disease shows a significant female predominance and strong HLA-B27 association in affected families
A founder mutation is exceptionally prevalent in Old Colony Mennonite and Hutterite populations, with carrier frequency reaching approximately 1 in 21 in some communities
Restrictive dermopathy occurs exclusively in African and Asian populations due to specific ethnic genetic variants
The condition demonstrates X-linked recessive inheritance, explaining the male predominance observed in clinical cohorts
questions.exp: Restrictive dermopathy shows no sex bias and has no HLA associations, as it is a purely monogenic Mendelian disorder of the nuclear envelope, not an immunological condition. A specific founder mutation is highly prevalent in the Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite and Hutterite populations in North America, with carrier status exceptionally high (up to 1 in 21 in Hutterite populations from South Dakota).

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with severe psoriasis is prescribed acitretin. She is counseled about teratogenicity and contraception. The patient mentions she enjoys a glass of wine with dinner. Which pharmacokinetic consequence is most critical to counsel regarding alcohol use?
opts: Alcohol inhibits CYP3A4, reducing acitretin metabolism and increasing serum concentrations to toxic levels
Alcohol causes reverse esterification of acitretin back to etretinate, which is highly lipophilic and accumulates in adipose tissue with a prolonged half-life of 80–160 days
Alcohol displaces acitretin from protein binding, causing rapid renal clearance and loss of efficacy
Alcohol increases the bioavailability of acitretin by 200%, mimicking the effect of a high-fat meal
questions.exp: Acitretin undergoes reverse esterification in the presence of alcohol, converting back to etretinate, which is highly lipophilic and deposits into adipose tissue. This dramatically extends the half-life to 80–160 days compared to acitretin's typical 50-hour half-life, creating prolonged teratogenic exposure and requiring extended contraception after drug discontinuation.

questions.q: A patient receiving rituximab for granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) demonstrates a reduced serum concentration despite appropriate dosing. The oncology team attributes this to a high CD20+ cell burden. Which pharmacokinetic principle best explains this observation?
opts: Linear pharmacokinetics with first-order elimination independent of target antigen expression
Non-linear pharmacokinetics where the half-life increases as CD20+ cell burden decreases and the available antigen sink becomes depleted
Rapid hepatic metabolism preventing adequate serum accumulation regardless of dosing interval
Renal filtration of intact rituximab molecules proportional to glomerular filtration rate
questions.exp: Rituximab exhibits non-linear pharmacokinetics influenced by the target antigen load (CD20 expression on B cells). A high CD20+ cell burden acts as an 'antigen sink,' causing rapid consumption and clearance of rituximab from circulation, resulting in lower serum concentrations. As B-cell numbers deplete with successive doses, this sink diminishes and serum levels increase.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with a 20-year history of varicose veins presents with an eczematous eruption on his left lower leg. The clinical presentation includes erythematous plaques with scaling, localized edema, and mild pigmentary changes. Which of the following conditions is the strongest independent risk factor for the development of stasis dermatitis in this patient?
opts: Prolonged standing occupation and obesity
Prior deep vein thrombosis with post-thrombotic syndrome
Concurrent atopic dermatitis
Recent exposure to irritant contact allergens
questions.exp: Among the modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for stasis dermatitis, a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) leading to post-thrombotic syndrome is the strongest predictor of subsequent venous insufficiency and stasis dermatitis development. While age, obesity, and prolonged immobility are significant risk factors, DVT-related valve incompetence creates the most severe and persistent venous hypertension.

questions.q: A 6-week-old male infant is referred for evaluation of large, dark-brown, tightly adherent polygonal scales affecting his neck, preauricular region, and flexural areas. The parents report the child was born covered with a collodion-like membrane that shed after 2 weeks. Laboratory testing reveals elevated maternal serum cholesterol sulfate. Which systemic complication should be screened for in this patient?
opts: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca and retinal dystrophy
Comma-shaped corneal opacities and cryptorchidism
Hepatic cirrhosis and pancreatic insufficiency
Neurological deterioration and seizure disorder
questions.exp: The clinical presentation of dark-brown scales affecting flexures and neck with involvement of a collodion phenotype at birth, combined with elevated cholesterol sulfate, is diagnostic of recessive X-linked ichthyosis (RXLI) caused by steroid sulfatase deficiency. Up to 50% of affected males develop asymptomatic comma-shaped corneal opacities on the posterior lens capsule, and there is a 20-fold increased risk of cryptorchidism with independent risk for testicular cancer.
questions.🏰 Palace: 🏰 Palace: A DIRTY NECK PRINCE (RXLI) sits in a CASTLE surrounded by CHOLESTEROL SULFATE moat—he wears COMMA-SHAPED SPECTACLES (opacities) and has a MISSING TESTICLE (cryptorchidism) that's tucked away in the tower (20-fold risk).

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with pruritic bite lesions on her arms and trunk. Upon examination of her mattress seams, you observe dark brown to black ink-like specks and shed translucent exoskeletons. Which of the following statements about the causative organism is correct?
opts: Cimex lectularius is found exclusively in tropical climates and has fully developed wings
The organism undergoes 5 nymphal instars, each requiring a blood meal to progress to the next stage
Adult bed bugs can survive indefinitely without a host due to their extremely efficient metabolic rate
The bite causes immediate pain and awakens the host due to the organism's salivary irritants
questions.exp: Bed bugs undergo exactly 5 nymphal instars over approximately 6 weeks, and every single life stage is haematophagous, requiring a blood meal to successfully moult to the next stage. Cimex lectularius is cosmopolitan and found in temperate climates (not exclusively tropical), they are wingless with only vestigial forewings, bites are painless due to anaesthetic and anticoagulant in saliva, and adults can survive up to 1 year (not indefinitely) without feeding.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with early brown age spots and parallel smile lines that are only visible during facial animation. According to the Glogau photoaging classification, what is the most appropriate treatment approach?
opts: Preventative care with superficial chemical peels and topical cosmeceuticals alone
Medium-depth chemical peels combined with topical retinoids and alpha-hydroxy acids
Deep resurfacing with ablative laser only
Observation without intervention as this represents normal aging
questions.exp: This clinical presentation—solar lentigines and wrinkles only visible with animation—defines Glogau Type II photoaging (early to moderate), typically seen in patients in their late 30s to 40s. Type II requires medium-depth chemical peels plus long-term topical retinoids and alpha-hydroxy acids. Superficial treatments alone (Type I) are insufficient for Type II severity, while deep resurfacing is reserved for Type III or IV disease.

questions.q: A neonate with suspected Ritter's disease (generalised SSSS) is found to have a focal nasopharyngeal colonization with Staphylococcus aureus phage group II strain 71. Which of the following best explains how this localized infection leads to widespread epidermal cleavage?
opts: Direct bacterial dissemination through the bloodstream with organism colonization in all epidermal layers
Haematogenous dissemination of exfoliative toxins (ETA/ETB) produced at the focal site, causing Dsg1 cleavage throughout the epidermis
Bacterial lipopolysaccharides triggering a systemic autoimmune response against epidermal cadherins
Toxins are produced in the dermis and migrate centrifugally to the stratum corneum
questions.exp: In generalised SSSS, the causative Staphylococcus aureus remains localized at a distant focal site (nasopharynx, conjunctiva, umbilicus, etc.) where it elaborates exfoliative toxins ETA and ETB. These toxins then disseminate haematogenously throughout the body, targeting and cleaving Desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis, creating a split at or within the stratum granulosum.

questions.q: A patient infested with bed bugs (Cimex hemipterus) asks why pesticide treatments sometimes fail despite multiple applications. Which of the following biological characteristics best explains this clinical challenge?
opts: Bed bugs possess fully developed wings allowing rapid escape and reinfestation from neighboring areas
Adult bed bugs can survive an average of 70 days and up to a full year without a blood meal, making them extremely difficult to eradicate through starvation strategies
Bed bugs are strictly host-specific to humans and cannot survive on alternative hosts, limiting the scope of control measures
Nymphal stages do not require blood meals and can complete their life cycle without feeding, creating hidden reservoirs
questions.exp: The extreme starvation resistance of bed bugs—surviving an average of 70 days and up to one year without a host—makes eradication extremely difficult and prolonged treatment strategies necessary. Bed bugs are wingless (cannot fly), they are NOT host-specific and will feed on other mammals and birds if needed, and all life stages including nymphs are haematophagous and require blood meals.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with fine, white-to-gray flaky scales on his extensor surfaces that worsen in winter and improve in summer. Physical examination reveals hyperlinear palms and soles, keratosis pilaris, and notably clear skin in the antecubital fossae. Histopathology shows orthohyperkeratosis with a diminished stratum granulosum. Which genetic mutation best explains this clinical presentation?
opts: Loss-of-function mutation in the STS gene on chromosome Xp22.3
Loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene on chromosome 1q21
Deletion of the ABCA12 gene on chromosome 2q35
Mutation in the TGM1 gene on chromosome 14q11.2
questions.exp: The clinical presentation of fine white-gray scales on extensor surfaces that spare flexures, combined with hyperlinear palms, keratosis pilaris, atopic diathesis, and the pathognomonic histological finding of a diminished stratum granulosum, is diagnostic of ichthyosis vulgaris. This disorder results from loss-of-function mutations in the FLG gene encoding filaggrin, which is critical for keratin aggregation in the stratum granulosum and production of natural moisturizing factors.
questions.🏰 Palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine FILAGGRIN as tiny GLUE holding bricks (keratins) in the GRANULOSUM castle floor—when FLG mutates, the glue breaks, flakes scatter on EXTENSOR WALLS, but the FLEXURE dungeons stay pristine because they're moist and humid.

questions.q: During rituximab therapy for pemphigus vulgaris, B-cell lysis is achieved primarily through three mechanisms. Which of the following statements about CD20 as a therapeutic target is INCORRECT?
opts: CD20 is expressed on pre-B cells, immature B cells, mature B cells, and memory B cells but NOT on plasma cells
CD20 undergoes rapid internalization and shedding upon rituximab binding, reducing antibody efficacy
CD20 is a transmembrane phosphoprotein whose precise physiological role in B-cell function remains partially unclear
CD20 is absent on hematopoietic stem cells and pro-B cells, allowing for B-cell regeneration after depletion
questions.exp: CD20 does NOT undergo internalization or shedding upon antibody binding—this stability is precisely what makes it an ideal therapeutic target. CD20 is stably expressed on the B-cell surface from the pre-B cell stage through memory B cells but is absent on plasma cells and stem cells, allowing for eventual reconstitution.

questions.q: A 62-year-old woman presents with eczematous plaques on the medial aspect of both lower legs, accompanied by edema and hyperpigmentation. She has a history of deep vein thrombosis 10 years ago. On examination, the skin is inflamed and weeping. She has been applying a topical antibiotic ointment for 2 weeks without improvement. Which diagnostic approach is most critical to establish the diagnosis and guide further management?
opts: Skin biopsy to rule out mycosis fungoides
Patch testing to exclude superimposed allergic contact dermatitis
Doppler ultrasonography to assess current DVT status
Fungal culture to rule out tinea corporis
questions.exp: Stasis dermatitis presents on the lower extremities in the setting of chronic venous insufficiency. Because the inflamed skin is highly susceptible to sensitization from topical medicaments, patch testing is strictly required to definitively exclude superimposed allergic contact dermatitis, which frequently complicates stasis dermatitis and can impede healing.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, irritability, and exquisite skin tenderness followed by a scarlatiniform rash on the face spreading to intertriginous areas. Within 48 hours, large flaccid bullae develop with tissue-paper-like skin wrinkling and radial fissuring around the mouth and eyes. Intraoral mucosa remains completely intact. Which molecular mechanism best explains the mucosal sparing despite extensive periorificial involvement?
opts: Mucous membranes lack Desmoglein-1 and rely primarily on Desmoglein-3, which is unaffected by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins
Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins are inactivated by salivary enzymes before reaching the intraoral epithelium
Mucous membranes have a thicker stratum corneum that prevents toxin penetration
Intraoral mucosal cells express human leukocyte antigen variants that neutralize exfoliative toxins
questions.exp: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins (ETA/ETB) are glutamate-specific serine proteases that specifically cleave Desmoglein-1 (Dsg1) located in superficial epidermal desmosomes. Mucous membranes rely on Desmoglein-3 for cell-to-cell adhesion, which is completely unaffected by these toxins, resulting in absolute mucosal sparing despite severe cutaneous involvement.

questions.q: A neonate with a congenital haemangioma on the forehead shows rapid regression beginning at 4 weeks of age, with complete involution expected by 12 months. The parents are counselled about likely residual findings. Which complication is most commonly left after involution of this lesion type?
opts: Persistent erythema and telangiectasia requiring laser therapy
Redundant, atrophic, hypopigmented skin
Progressive hypertrophy proportionate to growth
High risk of malignant transformation
questions.exp: A rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma (RICH) undergoes swift postnatal regression beginning within days to weeks of birth and is usually complete by 14 months. Affected infants are frequently left with redundant, atrophic, hypopigmented skin as the residuum. This distinguishes RICH from non-involuting variants and infantile haemangiomas.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: RICH tumours are like SPEED RACERS that ZIP through the castle hallway fast, then leave behind WRINKLED, DEFLATED BALLOONS (redundant atrophic skin) and GHOSTLY PALE FOOTPRINTS (hypopigmentation) — involution complete by 14 months!

questions.q: A 62-year-old man with history of asthma and eosinophilia develops necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract along with necrotizing vasculitis affecting small vessels. Which ANCA-associated vasculitis is this clinical presentation most consistent with?
opts: Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)
Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA)
Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane (Anti-GBM) Disease
questions.exp: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA, formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome) is characterized by eosinophil-rich and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation often involving the respiratory tract, combined with necrotizing vasculitis of small vessels, typically in patients with asthma history. MPA lacks granulomatous features; GPA is not eosinophil-predominant; Anti-GBM disease is immune-complex mediated, not ANCA-associated granulomatous vasculitis.

questions.q: A 2-week-old male presents with a fully formed, protuberant vascular tumour on his left thigh that was present at birth. Laboratory testing reveals the lesion is GLUT1-negative. Which genetic mutation most likely drives this congenital haemangioma?
opts: BRAF V600E mutation
GNAQ/GNA11 Gln209 missense mutation
TP53 loss-of-function mutation
PTEN haploinsufficiency
questions.exp: Congenital haemangiomas are driven by somatic activating missense mutations in GNAQ and GNA11 genes, specifically at glutamine amino acid 209 (Gln209), which constitutively upregulates the MAPK pathway and drives prenatal tumour growth. GLUT1-negativity is a key distinguishing feature from infantile haemangiomas. The same Gln209 mutation is shared across all three phenotypes (RICH, NICH, PICH).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a GNARLY QUEEN (GNAQ/GNA11) sitting at position 209 on a massive castle throne, forcing the MAPK pathway guards to work overtime BEFORE the baby is born — the tumour is fully cooked in utero, not after!

questions.q: A neonate presents at day 10 of life with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the scalp at the site of a fetal scalp electrode, along with keratoconjunctivitis and oral ulcers. The infant is otherwise well with no fever or neurologic signs. Which classification best describes this presentation?
opts: Congenital intrauterine HSV infection
Skin-Eye-Mouth (SEM) disease
Disseminated neonatal HSV with CNS involvement
Perinatal herpes with visceral organ involvement
questions.exp: This clinical picture—grouped vesicles at sites of birth trauma, keratoconjunctivitis, and ulcerative stomatitis presenting at day 10—is the classic presentation of Skin-Eye-Mouth (SEM) disease, which manifests between days 1-2 weeks of life with infection strictly limited to stratified squamous epithelium (skin, conjunctiva, oral mucosa) and sparing the CNS and visceral organs. The 0% mortality rate of isolated SEM disease and absence of systemic signs confirm this diagnosis.

questions.q: Which UV-induced mechanism is responsible for the paradoxical upregulation of abnormal elastin accumulation in photoaging, resulting in solar elastosis?
opts: UVB directly stimulates elastin gene transcription in dermal fibroblasts without concurrent ROS production

UVA-induced oxidative stress upregulates elastin synthesis while simultaneously activating elastase and cathepsin K; aged fibroblasts fail to clear fragmented elastin, leading to basophilic elastotic material accumulation
Intrinsic aging alone causes elastin degradation independent of UV exposure
UVA increases TGF-β signaling, which promotes uncontrolled elastin deposition
questions.exp: Solar elastosis is a hallmark of photoaging caused by a paradoxical process: UVA-induced ROS upregulates elastin synthesis while simultaneously activating degradative enzymes (elastase and cathepsin K). However, aged fibroblasts cannot efficiently clear the fragmented elastin pieces, resulting in massive accumulation of undegradable, abnormal, calcified basophilic elastotic material in the upper dermis. This contrasts with intrinsic aging, where normal elastic fibers simply degrade without excessive accumulation.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a chronic, painless ulcer on his genitalia that has not healed spontaneously over several months. Histopathology shows intracellular organisms with bipolar staining appearing as 'safety pins' within macrophage vacuoles. Which organism is responsible for this infection?
opts: Klebsiella granulomatis
Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3
Treponema pallidum
Haemophilus ducreyi
questions.exp: Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis or Donovania granulomatis) is the causative agent of donovanosis. The organism is identified as the Donovan body, a Gram-negative intracellular bacterium that displays characteristic bipolar ('safety-pin') staining and is found within vacuoles of macrophages or histiocytes.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SAFETY PIN with bipolar caps standing guard in a MACROPHAGE CASTLE ROOM—that's your K. granulomatis (Klebsiella) Donovan body, the intracellular sentinel of granuloma inguinale.

questions.q: A newborn presents with rigid, tightly adherent skin, severe joint contractures, and respiratory distress requiring intubation at 32 weeks gestation. Genetic testing reveals homozygous mutations in the ZMPSTE24 gene. What is the primary consequence of this molecular defect?
opts: Loss of lamin A and lamin C structural proteins due to failed gene transcription
Accumulation of toxic farnesylated prelamin A at the nuclear envelope due to failed post-translational cleavage
Autoimmune attack on nuclear lamina triggered by HLA-mediated T-cell activation
Defective collagen cross-linking in the dermis due to impaired lysyl oxidase activity
questions.exp: ZMPSTE24 encodes a zinc metallopeptidase essential for cleaving farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A. Without this enzymatic activity, toxic unprocessed prelamin A accumulates at the nuclear envelope, distorting nuclear morphology and disrupting global DNA replication and RNA transcription. This toxic accumulation of prelamin A—not loss of lamin proteins themselves—is the pathological hallmark of ZMPSTE24-mutated restrictive dermopathy.

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl with a painful plantar wart on her heel is found on histology to have massive orthokeratosis, endophytic growth, and prominent large eosinophilic keratohyalin inclusion granules. Which clinical variant and causative HPV type does this represent?
opts: Mosaic warts caused by HPV-2
Myrmecia caused by HPV-1
Flat warts caused by HPV-3
Filiform warts caused by HPV-4
questions.exp: Myrmecia is a specific variant of deep, highly painful plantar warts caused almost exclusively by HPV-1. The histological finding of prominent large eosinophilic keratohyalin inclusion granules is characteristic of myrmecia. Mosaic warts (HPV-2) are formed from coalescent superficial plantar warts, lack these granules, and are less painful than myrmecia.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: MYRMECIA sounds like 'ARMY'—imagine an ARMY of ANTS (the painful tumor-like warts) marching into the deep HEEL, each carrying giant GRANULES like ammunition; caused by HPV-1 (the ONE ant colony).

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with inflammatory markers elevated and imaging reveals stenosis of the left subclavian artery and descending thoracic aorta. She is suspected to have a large-vessel vasculitis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on her age and vessel involvement pattern?
opts: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)
Takayasu Arteritis (TAK)
Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)
questions.exp: Takayasu Arteritis (TAK) is a granulomatous arteritis of the aorta and its major branches with onset typically in patients <50 years, making it the most likely diagnosis in a young woman. Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is ruled out as it typically affects patients >50 years. PAN and GPA are not large-vessel vasculitides.

questions.q: Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy from a child with juvenile plantar dermatosis shows mild spongiosis and acanthosis. Which anatomical structure is the KEY distinguishing histological finding that localizes the inflammatory infiltrate?
opts: Sebaceous glands in the dermis
Acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts
Hair follicle infundibulum
Dermal-epidermal basement membrane zone
questions.exp: While juvenile plantar dermatosis shows non-specific chronic eczematous changes, the key distinguishing histological feature is inflammation specifically targeting the acrosyringium (sweat duct opening) and eccrine sweat ducts themselves. This reflects the pathophysiologic mechanism of hyperhidrosis and sweat-induced maceration driving the disease. The characteristic sweat duct involvement differentiates JPD from other childhood foot dermatitides.
